title: Inverse transformations: rewind the motion
explanation:
Solving $A\,x=v$ asks: which input arrow lands on $v$? Geometrically, play the transformation backwards. That reverse motion is itself a linear transformation, the inverse $A^{-1}$ [1], and $x=A^{-1}v$. Doing $A$ and then $A^{-1}$ (in either order) leaves every vector where it started.

Rewinding only works if nothing was lost. When $\det A=0$, the map squishes the plane onto a line (or a point); information is lost, and there is no inverse [2]. As 3Blue1Brown puts it, you cannot unsquish a line to turn it into a plane [3].

In practice: solve the two equations hidden in $A\,x=v$, then always check by multiplying $A$ times your answer.
keyIdeas: An inverse exists exactly when $\det A\ne0$.

steps: Check invertibility: $\det=2\cdot1-1\cdot1=1\ne0$, so exactly one solution exists.

pitfalls: Assuming every square matrix has an inverse; $\det=0$ rules it out.
Inverting entry by entry ($a\to1/a$), which only works for diagonal matrices.
Skipping the check: multiply back to confirm you land on the target.

citations.quote: When you play the transformation in reverse, it actually corresponds with a separate linear transformation, commonly called the inverse of A
But when the determinant is zero, and the transformation associated with the system of equations squishes space into a smaller dimension, there is no inverse.
You cannot unsquish a line to turn it into a plane.
